title: The Border Incident

narrative.text: The Military Command Center is a room built for bad news. Maps cover every wall. The radio console hums with encrypted traffic. Two aides are at the signal station, silent, their faces lit by the green glow of the radar screens. Colonel Dusek is at the main map table. She does not turn when the door opens.
Northern border. Three aircraft. Turned back forty minutes ago.
She traces a line on the map — a flight path that cuts through Gravenmark airspace and back again, precise as a surgeon's incision.
This one held position for eleven minutes.
She turns now. Her face is unreadable — the particular expression of someone who has already calculated the implications and is waiting to see whether you arrive at the same conclusion independently.
They wanted us to see them.
I identified the aircraft type at fourteen kilometers by silhouette. I know the flight profile. I know the pilot's unit by the registration visible in the photograph. This was reconnaissance.

Colonel Dusek is standing. Everyone else in the room — Vyktor, two aides, a signals officer — is seated. She is not pacing. She is planted. You enter and the room's gravity shifts toward you, but Dusek does not sit down.

Colonel Dusek does not usually come to the palace. She prefers her command post at the Defense Ministry, where the maps are current to the hour and the communications staff can reach any battalion commander in ninety seconds. When she appears in the situation room at seven in the evening, still in field uniform, you know before she speaks that something has happened on the border.

At 14:37 today, two Tyvaren fighter-bombers crossed into Veltrian airspace at the Gravenmark Pass. Overflight altitude: eight hundred meters. They circled twice. They photographed our defensive positions. Total violation: six minutes, forty-three seconds. The garrison commander at Checkpoint Seven held fire. I reviewed his decision. I support it. Here is what the Chancellor needs to know: Marshal Vukov will now deny the incursion occurred while simultaneously dispatching a diplomatic note accusing Veltria of fabricating the incident to justify escalation. That is his pattern. Provocation. Denial. Counter-accusation. He has executed it six times since 1958. This was the seventh.

She places a photograph on the table. A Tyvaren fighter-bomber, clearly marked with the red hawk insignia of the Tyvaren Republican Air Force, banking over the snow-covered ridge of the Gravenmark Pass. The photograph is dated and time-stamped. The border checkpoint is visible in the background. There is no ambiguity about what happened.

Third airspace violation in fourteen months. The previous two occurred under Halvek. He filed private protests. Tyvaren ignored them. Vukov is now testing the new Chancellor. He wants the answer to one question: does Veltria's response change? Three options produce three outcomes. Protest through diplomatic channels — he continues the violations on a quarterly schedule. Scramble interceptors and match his posture at the pass — he escalates and blames Veltria for the escalation. Do nothing — next time he sends four aircraft instead of two and the overflight extends to eleven minutes. There is a narrow corridor between weakness and provocation. The Chancellor must choose where the line is drawn.

Dusek is giving me the military option without asking for it. That is restraint — the kind of restraint that comes from having seen what happens when restraint fails. She held the garrison commander's fire and she is telling me that the decision about what to do next is political, not military. She is also telling me, in the careful language of a professional soldier who cannot tell her civilian commander what to do, that Vukov will not stop at airspace violations. He will keep pushing until he finds the line. I have to decide where the line is — and what I am willing to do when he crosses it.

Before you speak, you look at Dusek — really look at her. She is standing at attention, but something in her posture is different. Less rigid. More... present. You ask her directly: 'Colonel. Your personal recommendation. Not the Defense Ministry's. Yours.'
It is the first time you have asked her for a personal opinion rather than a military assessment. She does not answer immediately. When she does, her voice is quieter than you have ever heard it.

Stand down. The garrison commander held fire. That was correct. Scramble interceptors and we manufacture a provocation. Accept a provocation and we authorize a response. Authorize a response and we begin an escalation cycle that ends exactly one way. I have seen where that road ends, Chancellor. It ends in fields. In my first command — a border post south of here, seventeen years ago — we had a similar incident. Halvek ordered us to match force with force. By the end of that week, fourteen Veltrian soldiers were dead. Two Tyvaren pilots. One village. No strategic gain. No territorial change. Fourteen funerals and a promotion for the general who gave the order. I attended every funeral. The general did not attend any. So. My personal recommendation. Stand down. Use the photograph. Use the diplomatic channel. Use anything except the interceptors. That is not the military assessment. That is the assessment of someone who has written the letters to fourteen families.

monologue: Dusek held the garrison commander's fire. That's restraint — the kind that comes from having seen what happens when restraint fails. Six minutes and forty-three seconds. Two fighter-bombers photographing our defensive positions. Vukov will deny it happened while accusing us of fabricating it. That's his pattern — provocation, denial, counter-accusation. He's testing whether the new Chancellor's response differs from the old one. The answer has to be yes. The question is how.

choices.text: "I want the photograph published. Every newspaper in Veltria, every foreign correspondent in Ashenmere. A formal diplomatic protest delivered to the Tyvaren embassy within the hour, and a copy sent to the International Forum in Stellamere. Vukov wants to test me in private? Fine. I'll answer him in public. The world will see what his pilots did over the Gravenmark. Let him deny a photograph."

reactions.text: She does not sit. She reaches for the photograph, turns it toward the light, examines it once more. The examination is not about the photograph. It is about the decision. She is satisfied.
Public. Good. Let the photograph do the work. The world will see what happened. Vukov's denial will be the story — not the violation. The diplomatic note goes to the embassy within the hour.
Press release being drafted. International correspondents notified. The photograph will lead every front page by morning. Vukov wanted a test in private. He is receiving an answer in public.

choices.text: "No public statement yet. Send the diplomatic note through the backchannel we established with Tyvaren's foreign ministry in Week One. Tell them we have the photograph but are choosing not to publish it — this time. Make clear that the next violation will be met with a formal complaint to the International Forum and a request for neutral observers at the border. Offer a direct line between Dusek and her Tyvaren counterpart to prevent future 'misunderstandings.' Give Vukov a way to de-escalate without losing face."

reactions.text: They'll do it again next week.
The Arcturian ambassador will want a statement.
History suggests that restraint here reads as an invitation. I note that I have been wrong before.

choices.text: "Move a battalion to the Gravenmark Pass. Not to engage — to be seen. Dusek, I want the Tyvarens to see Veltrian soldiers on the border, visibly reinforced, visibly prepared. No shooting. No provocation. Presence. The next pilot who flies over our airspace should see anti-aircraft positions that were not there last week and wonder whether they want to test whether they are operational. Vukov will understand the message. He speaks military. So will we."

reactions.text: She picks up the phone before you finish speaking.
That will require a public explanation.
